content.title: Solving Right Triangles for Angle of Elevation and Depression
content.overview: This lesson focuses on using the tangent ratio to solve for unknown heights or distances in real-world scenarios involving angles of elevation and depression. By modeling these situations as right triangles, you can efficiently calculate vertical heights using horizontal distances and vice versa.
learning_objectives: Define and identify angles of elevation and depression in a geometric context.
Model real-world height and distance problems using right triangles.
Apply the tangent ratio (tan θ = opposite / adjacent) to solve for unknown side lengths.
Differentiate between the horizontal distance (adjacent) and the vertical height (opposite).

sections.title: Defining Elevation and Depression
sections.content:
An angle of elevation is the angle formed between a horizontal line of sight and the line of sight up to an object. An angle of depression is the angle formed between a horizontal line of sight and the line of sight down to an object. Crucially, both angles are measured from the horizontal. In a right triangle model, the horizontal distance from the observer to the object acts as the 'adjacent' leg, while the vertical height of the object acts as the 'opposite' leg.

![A right triangle where the base is labeled 'Horizontal Distance (Adjacent)', the vertical side is 'Height (Opposite)', and the angle at the base is 'Angle of Elevation'.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/674ad56e-2121-4d6e-9249-fed3b0638708-1786505984620-81.webp)

sections.title: The Tangent-Form Solve Strategy
sections.content: When a problem provides a horizontal distance and an angle to find a height, the tangent ratio is the most direct tool. The formula is: tan(θ) = opposite / adjacent. To solve for the height (opposite), rearrange the formula to: Height = Horizontal Distance × tan(θ). If you are given the height and need the horizontal distance, the formula becomes: Horizontal Distance = Height / tan(θ).

worked_examples.question: A surveyor stands 80 feet away from the base of a building. The angle of elevation from the ground where the surveyor is standing to the top of the building is 40°. What is the height of the building to the nearest foot?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the components. The horizontal distance (adjacent leg) is 80 ft. The angle θ is 40°. The height (opposite leg) is h. Step 2: Set up the tangent equation: tan(40°) = h / 80. Step 3: Solve for h by multiplying both sides by 80: h = 80 × tan(40°). Step 4: Calculate the value. tan(40°) ≈ 0.839. h = 80 × 0.839 = 67.12. Step 5: Round to the nearest foot. The building is approximately 67 feet tall.

common_mistakes: Confusing the hypotenuse with the horizontal distance; the horizontal ground is always the adjacent leg.
Using sine or cosine instead of tangent when the hypotenuse is not involved.
Measuring the angle of depression from a vertical line (like a wall) instead of the horizontal line of sight.
Forgetting to ensure the calculator is in Degree mode rather than Radian mode.
exam_tips: Always draw a quick sketch to visualize the right triangle and label the 'opposite' and 'adjacent' sides relative to the given angle.
Remember that the angle of elevation from Point A to Point B is equal to the angle of depression from Point B to Point A because they are alternate interior angles.
If the answer choices contain 'tan', you likely do not need to calculate a decimal value; just set up the algebraic expression.
content.recap: To solve elevation and depression problems, identify the horizontal distance as the adjacent side and the vertical height as the opposite side of a right triangle. Use the tangent ratio (tan θ = opp/adj) to solve for the missing variable, ensuring your angle is measured from the horizontal.

knowledge_claims.content: An angle of elevation is the angle between a horizontal line and the line of sight looking up at an object.
An angle of depression is the angle between a horizontal line and the line of sight looking down at an object.
In elevation and depression problems, the horizontal distance from the observer to the object represents the adjacent leg of a right triangle.
In elevation and depression problems, the vertical height of the object represents the opposite leg of a right triangle.
The tangent ratio formula used for these problems is tan(θ) = opposite / adjacent.
To find the height when given the horizontal distance and angle, multiply the horizontal distance by the tangent of the angle.
The angle of elevation from an observer to an object is equal in measure to the angle of depression from the object back to the observer.
A common error is using the sine ratio (opposite/hypotenuse) when only the horizontal distance (adjacent) and height (opposite) are provided.
Always verify that the angle of depression is measured from a horizontal line of sight, not from the vertical object itself.
If an object is very tall relative to the horizontal distance, the angle of elevation will be greater than 45 degrees because the tangent of angles > 45° is greater than 1.
To solve for the horizontal distance when height and angle are known, divide the height by the tangent of the angle.
The line of sight between the observer and the object represents the hypotenuse of the right triangle.
